cells.tense: You are here with the work, reading how the pieces actually fit.
cells.ask: Say out loud what you see holding the whole thing together, once, to one person working on it with you. Let them add or correct.
cells.core:
The work is in your hands and you can read how its parts meet. Not hovering above it, not buried in it — near enough to touch and far enough to see where it's already leaning. That reading is doing real work. It's why the thing goes up straight instead of getting corrected later.

What you're making needs more than one pair of hands, and you're not forcing it. You leave room for what other people bring. What you notice gets said, gets tested, gets adjusted. Seeing the whole and staying in the room where it gets built — that's the balance. The next thing it can feed is real: whoever hears it can carry part of it forward with you.
cells.sheetLine: You see the whole thing and you're still in the room building it.
cells.verb: raising the first structure more than one pair of hands can build
cells.place: standing just outside the system, still inside it, seeing what holds across all of it

cells.tense: You are already standing in the finished version of this, checking it for cracks that haven't opened yet.
cells.ask: Pick one piece that's actually in place today. Leave it alone for a day. Don't inspect it, don't brace it, don't explain it.
cells.core:
You're bracing at a thing not yet built. There's a version where the whole works, and you've moved into it early — scanning for flaws, what will break, who won't get it, where the joints will fail. Reading the pattern has turned into guarding it.

The building is happening. You're just not letting it happen without correcting it in advance. Every piece gets held up against a finished shape that doesn't exist, and the real work doesn't survive that much pre-checking. What's being built needs to be built, not defended before it's ready. Let one thing stand without your future eye on it, and see whether it holds on its own.

cells.tense: You stopped stepping back to look at the whole pattern, and the pieces have been coming at you one at a time since.
cells.ask: Name the single shape you want this to take in one sentence, to yourself or someone else. Then let that sentence be what you build toward this week.
cells.core:
You know how to see the whole thing, and you haven't been doing it. Everything is coming in pieces — this task, that problem, the next thing — and you're handling each one on its own. From where you're standing, nothing adds up to a shape.

You stopped stepping back at some point. Maybe looking at the whole thing was too much to hold. Either way, you're in the middle of a build without a picture of what it's for. Nothing's wrong with the hands. What's missing is the step back — the one that shows you what all this is making. Take the step, even for a minute. You don't have to like everything you see.

cells.tense: You are already shaping how the whole thing is understood, and you are calling it just how things turned out.
cells.ask: Name one choice you made this week that set the direction for the group, or the project, or the work. Say 'I chose that' out loud, once.
cells.core:
Reading the whole and saying what holds is something you do well — you spot how the pieces meet while the room is still arguing about one of them. When it's working, that reading gets said out loud and other people build on it.

Right now it's going unnamed. In how you frame things, what you point at, what you let stand, the shape of the whole is getting set by you, and you talk about it like it's just the situation. You're the one stepping back and saying what holds. A person can't build toward a pattern they haven't admitted they're setting. Name the choice, and something shifts.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim in my draft is that the person has been reading the whole pattern all along at the Unacknowledged status — the record gives me a capacity that is operating, not proof that they have seen anything. A reader could reasonably say the pattern they're seeing is a method I invented for them rather than something they already do. The ask survives a wrong read: each one asks for an act, not a felt insight, so a person who says 'no, that's not me' still has something concrete to try or refuse. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'you already know' — it flatters the reading and puts words in their mouth. Fixed by narrowing each status to a moment they could recognise and letting the ask stand on its own feet.
